original_item.title: Verify Indexer captures all IndexedTransfer events without loss
original_item.summary: Event capture integrity is self-verifying: missing events cause on-chain proof rejection. Off-chain audit required for operational assurance.

counterexample.1_input_validation_bypass: If indexer misses event, generated proof will fail on-chain verification (hash chain mismatch).
counterexample.3_resource_exhaustion: Each transfer requires gas payment, limiting spam rate. Indexer can process events asynchronously.
counterexample.5_race_conditions: Indexer processes reorged block, proof uses invalid hash chain, on-chain verification fails.

reviewed_items.reasoning: This is not an on-chain security issue. The Indexer is an off-chain service that assists users in generating proofs. Any failure in event capture, reorg handling, or data integrity is detected by on-chain verification. Specifically, line 282 in Verifier.sol enforces `require(expectedHashChain == newHashChain, NewHashChainMismatch(...))` which rejects proofs built on incorrect event data. The counterexamples describe operational failures (availability issues) not security vulnerabilities.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexamples describe off-chain operational failures, not on-chain attack vectors. Missing events cause proof generation to produce an incorrect hash chain, which is deterministically rejected by on-chain verification. There is no way for an attacker to exploit indexer failures to compromise on-chain security - only to cause denial of service for proof generation, which users can resolve by self-hosting the indexer.

guards_found.reason: On-chain hash chain verification ensures any incorrect indexer data results in proof rejection

guard_analysis.bypass_method: N/A - Off-chain component cannot bypass on-chain verification

proof_trace: Off-chain: Indexer watches blockchain for IndexedTransfer events
Off-chain: If event missed, Merkle tree has incorrect leaves
Off-chain: Proof generated with incorrect hash chain
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:280 - expectedHashChain loaded from reservedHashChains[newIndex]
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:282 - Proof rejected with NewHashChainMismatch if hash chain incorrect
Conclusion: On-chain guard prevents exploitation of off-chain failures
reviewed_items.false_positive_reason: The concern describes an operational availability issue, not a security vulnerability. On-chain verification (hash chain comparison at line 282 and ZK proof validation at line 275) provides complete protection against any off-chain data integrity issues. The attack surface is non-existent because off-chain components cannot bypass cryptographic verification.

original_item.title: Verify Indexer Merkle tree matches on-chain computation
original_item.summary: Algorithm mismatch between indexer and on-chain is self-correcting via proof verification failure. Requires off-chain code audit.

counterexample.1_input_validation_bypass: Indexer uses SHA-256 instead of on-chain algorithm -> proof fails on-chain verification.
counterexample.2_state_transition_violation: Incorrect tree root cannot pass on-chain hash chain verification.
counterexample.5_race_conditions: Race in tree update causes invalid proof, caught on-chain.

reviewed_items.reasoning: Algorithm mismatch between the off-chain indexer and on-chain verification is not a security vulnerability - it's a self-correcting implementation bug. If the indexer uses the wrong hash algorithm (e.g., SHA-256 vs Poseidon), the generated proofs will fail on-chain verification at lines 275 and 282 of Verifier.sol. An attacker cannot exploit this mismatch to steal funds or corrupt state; the worst case is denial of service for proof generation, which users can resolve by using a correctly-implemented indexer.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexamples describe implementation bugs that cause proofs to be rejected, not attack vectors. An attacker cannot weaponize indexer bugs because: (1) they cannot control the indexer's implementation, and (2) on-chain verification deterministically rejects invalid proofs regardless of how they were generated. The scenario 'indexer uses wrong algorithm' describes a software defect affecting availability, not a security vulnerability.

guards_found.reason: IRootDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof validates the cryptographic structure of proofs
Merkle root derived from incorrect tree will not match on-chain expected value

guard_analysis.bypass_method: N/A - ZK proof verification is cryptographically binding

proof_trace: Off-chain: Indexer builds Merkle tree from events
Off-chain: If wrong algorithm used, tree root is incorrect
Off-chain: Proof generated referencing incorrect root
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:267 - Proof decoded, extracting claimed root values
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:275 - ZK verification rejects proof with wrong structure
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:282 - Hash chain verification rejects incorrect Merkle computation
Conclusion: Cryptographic verification prevents any off-chain algorithm mismatch from causing security issues
reviewed_items.false_positive_reason: This is not a security issue but an implementation correctness concern. The on-chain ZK verifier (line 275) and hash chain comparison (line 282) provide complete protection. Even if the indexer implementation is buggy, the on-chain contracts will reject invalid proofs. The concern should be addressed as a software quality/testing issue, not a security vulnerability.

original_item.title: Verify STATE-INDEXER-TREE-READY implies on-chain consistency
original_item.summary: Indexer ready state is verified by on-chain proof submission. Off-chain audit needed for UX optimization.

counterexample.1_input_validation_bypass: Indexer claims ready with wrong root -> user generates proof -> on-chain rejects proof.
counterexample.2_state_transition_violation: False ready state only wastes user time generating invalid proofs.

reviewed_items.reasoning: The 'ready' state of the indexer is an advisory signal with no security implications. If the indexer falsely reports ready status with an inconsistent tree, the generated proof will be rejected by on-chain verification. The counterexample explicitly states this: 'on-chain rejects proof'. This is a UX/operational issue (user wastes time), not a security vulnerability. No funds can be stolen, no state can be corrupted.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexamples describe UX degradation scenarios, not security attacks. A false 'ready' state causes users to attempt proof generation that will fail, wasting time and gas. However, no security property is violated: on-chain verification (lines 275, 278, 282) will reject any proof generated from an inconsistent tree. The attacker gains nothing exploitable.

guards_found.reason: ZK proof verification and hash chain comparison reject all invalid proofs regardless of off-chain status signals

guard_analysis.bypass_method: N/A - On-chain verification is independent of off-chain status

proof_trace: Off-chain: Indexer sets 'tree ready' status (advisory signal)
Off-chain: User trusts status and generates proof
Off-chain: If tree actually inconsistent, proof has wrong data
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:275 - ZK verification catches cryptographic inconsistency
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:282 - Hash chain check catches Merkle inconsistency
On-chain: Transaction reverts, user loses gas but no funds stolen
Conclusion: False ready state causes UX issue, not security vulnerability
reviewed_items.false_positive_reason: The indexer's 'ready' state is purely informational and has no on-chain effect. On-chain security does not depend on off-chain status signals. The contracts verify proof validity independently through cryptographic verification, making this concern a UX/operational issue rather than a security vulnerability.

original_item.title: Verify Indexer generates valid Merkle inclusion proofs
original_item.summary: Proof validity is ultimately verified by on-chain ZK circuits. Off-chain audit ensures correct format.

counterexample.1_input_validation_bypass: Wrong sibling order in proof -> circuit verification fails.
counterexample.3_resource_exhaustion: DoS on indexer delays proofs but doesn't compromise security.
counterexample.4_faulty_error_handling: Failed proof generation -> user retry or error message.

reviewed_items.reasoning: Merkle inclusion proof generation is an off-chain operation with no on-chain attack surface. Invalid proofs (wrong sibling order, incorrect values, malformed structure) are rejected by the on-chain ZK verifier at line 275 (IRootDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof) and line 326/348 (IWithdrawDecider/IWithdrawVerifier). The counterexamples explicitly acknowledge this: 'circuit verification fails'. DoS on the indexer is an availability concern, not a security vulnerability.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexamples describe operational issues (proof generation failures, DoS) rather than security vulnerabilities. An attacker cannot exploit incorrect proof generation because: (1) invalid proofs are rejected on-chain, (2) DoS only delays users who can self-host the indexer, and (3) there is no way to make the on-chain contracts accept an invalid proof through indexer manipulation.

guards_found.reason: IRootDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof validates all proof components cryptographically

guard_analysis.bypass_method: N/A - ZK verification provides cryptographic soundness guarantees

proof_trace: Off-chain: Indexer generates Merkle inclusion proof
Off-chain: If proof has wrong sibling order or values, it's mathematically invalid
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:266-295 - proveTransferRoot entry point
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:275 - ZK verifier rejects invalid proof structure
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:326 or 348 - Teleport proofs also verified
Conclusion: Invalid proofs are deterministically rejected by on-chain verification
reviewed_items.false_positive_reason: Merkle proof correctness is enforced by on-chain ZK verification. The off-chain indexer cannot cause security issues because all proofs are cryptographically validated before any state change. This is an implementation quality concern (ensuring the indexer produces correctly-formatted proofs) rather than a security vulnerability.

original_item.title: Verify Decider-Prover service availability monitoring
original_item.summary: Prover service is optional - users can self-host. Availability is operational, not security-critical.

counterexample.1_input_validation_bypass: Service down -> users run local prover -> same security guarantees.

reviewed_items.reasoning: The Decider-Prover service is an optional off-chain convenience service. Its availability has no security implications because: (1) users can self-host the prover, (2) the prover only converts IVC proofs to Groth16 format which is verified on-chain, and (3) on-chain verification (lines 275, 326, 348) ensures proof validity regardless of which prover generated it. Service downtime is an availability/UX concern, not a security vulnerability.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample acknowledges that service unavailability does not compromise security: 'users run local prover -> same security guarantees'. This is correct. The prover service is a convenience that converts proof formats; it does not have any privileged access to on-chain state. Even a malicious prover service cannot compromise security because all outputs are verified on-chain.

guards_found.reason: All proofs are cryptographically verified on-chain regardless of which service generated them
Users can run their own prover, eliminating single point of failure

guard_analysis.bypass_method: N/A - Prover service has no privileged access; all outputs verified on-chain

proof_trace: Off-chain: Prover service converts IVC proofs to Groth16
Off-chain: Service unavailability prevents conversion (DoS)
Off-chain: User can self-host prover to generate same output
contracts/src/Verifier.sol:275,326,348 - On-chain verification validates all proofs
Conclusion: Service availability is operational concern, on-chain security unaffected
reviewed_items.false_positive_reason: Prover service availability monitoring is an operational/SRE concern, not a security vulnerability. The service has no special privileges - it merely performs a mathematical transformation (IVC to Groth16) that users can perform locally. On-chain verification ensures that even a compromised prover service cannot produce accepted invalid proofs.
